newsitem.title: USA: Kansas town takes lead in Anglo-U.S. pancake race.
newsitem.headline: Kansas town takes lead in Anglo-U.S. pancake race.

text.p: An annual trans-Atlantic contest was settled on Tuesday as Kansas schoolteacher Christina Wilbers won the Pancake Day footrace in 58.57 seconds, a time that beat the winner of a similar race held earlier in Britain.

Wilbers' victory meant Liberal, Kansas, took the lead in the series with Olney, England, which has held the Shrove Tuesday footrace on and off since 1445. Prior to Wilbers' win, the series had been tied at 23 wins apiece.
Housewife Avril Soman won this year's race in Olney with a time of 63.5 seconds.

The approximately 1/4-mile race tends to be dominated by women, who must follow a strict dress code of skirts, aprons and headscarves. Competitors must be able to whip up a pancake that can be tossed at the beginning and end of the race.
Event sponsors in Liberal said James Halley, a representative of the British consulate in Chicago, gave Wilbers the congratulatory "Kiss of Peace" after she finished first among 11 runners.
Wilbers, who ran track in college, also won last year's race. Mark Strange, a spokesman, said Wilbers' time of 58.57 seconds fell just shy of the 58.50-second record set in 1975.

Reverend Nigel Pond, who was at the finishing line outside St. Peter and St. Paul's Church in the small town of Olney in Buckinghamshire, in central England, said the event was a tradition held each year "come hell or high water."

Liberal's involvement in the race began 47 years ago after R.J. Leete, a civic leader, saw a magazine picture of the Olney women racing each other. He contacted Reverend Ronald Collins of St. Peter and St. Paul's Church in Olney and challenged the town's women to race against the women of Liberal. Collins replied: "The race is on!"
Winning scores have traded back and forth between the two towns. In 1980 the score did not count because the Olney finish line was blocked by a television truck.
Last year's race in Olney was almost cancelled because of a blizzard, but this year's event was held in good weather with only a light wind, Pond told Reuters.
Pancakes are traditionally eaten on Shrove Tuesday, the last day before the Lent pre-Easter fast.
